newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin fails to please everyone in keynote speech.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin fails to please everyone in keynote speech.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin's allies hailed his state of the nation address on Thursday as the combative leader's return to the political stage after months of absence from work caused by bad health.
But his political opponents, who have tried to remove him for health reasons, were not impressed and said it offered only empty promises which would not be fulfilled.
"I saw a tough Yeltsin, exactly the man we adored in 1987," Moscow Mayor Yuri Luzhkov said after Yeltsin's 25-minute speech to parliament.
Luzhkov was referring to the times when Yeltsin, then a silver-haired rebel, launched his crusade against communism.
Kremlin chief of staff Anatoly Chubais called it a clear programme of action and "an unprecedentedly tough assessment of the current situation".
Yeltsin, out of the Kremlin for much of the time since his re-election last July, appeared fit and aggressive. He rebuked his own government, promised government changes and vowed to curb crime.
But the leader of the influential opposition Communist Party, which dominates the State Duma (lower house of parliament), said the speech offered empty promises and no real solutions.

"It was another show," communist leader Gennady Zyuganov said. "It's nice to hear from the president that things are bad. But who is to blame for the situation when the economy is falling apart and people do not get their pay?"
"Yeltsin gave no idea about what he is going to do about it."
Communist Gennady Seleznyov, who is the chairmain of the Duma, was more sympathetic.
"This document is in tune with what we all feel," he said, referring to the text of a longer address on which the president's speech was based.
He said he was impressed by Yeltsin's call to impose order in Russia. "We are ready to follow the banner saying 'All powers to the law'," Seleznyov said.
Seleznyov, who is criticised by some communists for becoming part of Russia's political elite, also said he backed the need for changes in the government.
"I think changes will come because the president aims at creating a manageable economy, something we have rejected so far because it was part of the communist system," he said.

Yegor Gaidar, Yeltsin's former economic reform supremo but now a critic of the government, said Yeltsin's pledges to push ahead with a new tax code, liberalise land ownership and other promises gave Russia's stalled reforms a chance for a new start.
"There are some good points in the president's address which revive hope," he said. "But of course we have to wait and see when and if the words turn into deeds."
Yeltsin's approach won muted praise from some influential regional bosses in the Federation Council (upper chamber).

"We cannot but try to carry out (Yeltsin's) plan," said Eduard Rossel, governor of the Sverdlovsk region in the Urals. "He pointed out obvious things which just need to be done if we do not want the country to fall apart."
